newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS - Spain sanctions seventh rate cut of year.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Spain sanctions seventh rate cut of year.

text.p: The Bank of Spain, cheered by sluggish inflation, sanctioned its seventh interest rate cut of the year on Friday in a move which economists say paves the way for further hefty cuts well into next year.
The central bank said it had cut its key money rate half a point to 6.25 percent from 6.75 percent at its regular repurchase tender for central bank certificates.

"The 50 basis point cut was at the top end of expectations and is a sign that the central bank wants to get a decent amount of cutting in before the cycle turns late next year," said Luca Jellinek, bond stategist at Paribas in London.

Economists said November's inflation data, released minutes before the central bank announced the results of its tender, would have reassured the central bank that inflation was set on a downward trend.
November consumer price index (CPI) data was unchanged after a 0.1 percent rise in October. Year-on-year inflation rose 3.2 percent compared with 3.5 percent in October and 4.4 percent a year ago.

"The CPI data was better than the forecasts. This number allows us to close the year under 3.5-3.4 percent, which will allow the Bank of Spain to continue its policy of reducing the price of money," said Carmen Hernansanz, analyst at Merrill Lynch in Madrid.
The Bank of Spain has revised down its forecast for 1996 inflation to 3.4 percent from 3.5 percent, but some economists said year-end inflation could come in much lower.
"Inflation could end the year, overall and core, at 3.1 percent," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
Economists said the inflation data supported further sizeable cuts well into next year.
"Before spring, the central bank could lower another quarter to half-point and a little more in function of the expectations of joining EMU," said Fernandez.
Although analysts were clearly encouraged by the rate cut and inflation data, Spain's financial markets were not so overwhelmed and bonds slipped lower under a wave of profit taking.

"What we are seeing right now is a market selling on the fact. November CPI was better than expected, and when we saw it before the Bank of Spain, we were convinced that the Bank of Spain would cut the key rate," said Antonio Mielgo, economist at Bnka of America in Madrid.
Economists said the bond market had bought heavily after the CPI data which the market interpreted as a sure sign that money rates would be cut.
The peseta, however, was not shaken and stood firm in the narrow trading range seen in recent sessions.
By 1115 GMT, the peseta stood at 84.22 per mark, compared with 84.21 seen earlier in the session and 84.23 in late trade on Thursday.
Economists said in the medium term, however, markets would recover their enthusiasm for further rate cuts.

"The Spanish market is pretty well supported and this support comes from the fundamentals...I think we're not so vulnerable in the medium term," said Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
Commerical banks were also encouraged by the rate cut, and followed suit with reductions in their prime rates.

Banco Santander slashed half-a-point off its prime rate to eight percent, while Argentaria and Banesto cut their prime rates half-a-point to 7.75 percent. BBV also cut its prime rate half-a-point to 8.50 percent.
